title: 'Flock Flocked up'

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated licence plate reader, compounded by what happened after the alert. The camera matched a plate to a stolen vehicle record when the plate in fact belonged to a different car, and the traffic stop that followed was executed on the strength of that single alert. The failure sits at the front of the deployment: an automated identification system produced a confident match, and officers acted on it as though it were verified. Nothing in the reporting shows the system flagged its own uncertainty or that anyone checked the read against the vehicle before the stop.

The second failure is one of escalation rather than identification. A wrong alert is recoverable, and the officers confirmed the plate was not stolen once they were face to face with the driver. By then guns were drawn and a K-9 handler had moved in. The department's own policy required handlers to weigh threat and active resistance before deploying a dog, which means the decision point was a human judgement made under the influence of the bad alert. Catching this would have required either a verification step between the camera alert and the stop, or a check that treated the alert as a lead rather than a fact.

What is not established is whether the camera's error rate was known to the department, whether the officers' conduct violated policy, and what the outcome of the investigation into those officers will be. An internal finding of no wrongdoing is not a finding that the stop was correct, and dropped charges are not a verdict on the arrest.

reports.title: Body cam of TPD officers releasing K-9 on man during traffic stop
Man speaks out after police release K-9 on him during traffic stop: 'Traumatized'
TPD investigation finds no wrongdoing in use of K-9 on man during traffic stop
Charges dropped against man Toledo Police released K-9 on during traffic stop, lawyer says

summary:
Toledo Police released body camera video showing officers stopping a red Dodge Ram pickup after a FLOCK camera alert about a stolen license plate. The alert was wrong, as the camera misread a plate that belonged to a Chevy Malibu. Officers approached with guns drawn and ordered driver Brandon Upchurch out of the truck. He exited with his hands up, then walked toward the grass, and a K-9 handler moved closer with the dog.

Upchurch was arrested and charged with resisting arrest and obstruction. Officers later confirmed the plate was not stolen and that the camera had misread it. He received medical attention at the scene. Police said they thought he might flee and did not know if he or the passenger had weapons. Multiple TPD officers are under investigation, and the department's K-9 policy requires handlers to weigh factors like threat and active resistance before deploying a dog.
